title: Obstructive and Motility Disorders of the Gastrointestinal Tract
subject: Gastrointestinal System (GAST)
author: Dr. Sharilyn Rennie

overview.intro: This chapter covers conditions that stop contents from moving through the gut, from the pharynx to the rectum. Some are failures of nerves or muscle (achalasia, adynamic ileus, Hirschsprung disease, gastroparesis), and some are physical blocks (hernias, intussusception, volvulus, adhesions). Board questions usually describe a patient by age, history, and one or two signs, such as a bird-beak esophagus, currant jelly stool, or an empty rectal vault, and ask for the mechanism or the expected finding. If you can say whether the problem is neural, muscular, or mechanical, and whether the blood supply is threatened, you can reason through most of these questions.
prerequisites: Layers of the gut wall and the location of the myenteric and submucosal plexuses (GI-2)
Enteric neurotransmitters: acetylcholine and substance P (excitatory), nitric oxide and VIP (inhibitory) (GI-6)
Peristalsis, receptive relaxation, and the migrating motor complex (GI-6)
Midgut rotation and neural crest migration (GI-1)
Inguinal canal, femoral canal, and esophageal hiatus anatomy (GI-4)

connections.how: Hirschsprung disease and midgut volvulus with malrotation are failures of neural crest migration and gut rotation.
Trypanosoma cruzi destroys the enteric plexus, and Clostridioides difficile colitis can progress to toxic megacolon.
Strangulation and volvulus cause bowel infarction by the same ischemic pathway as mesenteric vascular occlusion.
Ulcerative colitis is the classic setting of toxic megacolon, and reflux is the main consequence of a sliding hiatal hernia.
Vomiting and fluid sequestration in obstruction cause hypovolemia, hypokalemia, and metabolic alkalosis, and hypokalemia itself worsens ileus.

terms.def: The network of enteric ganglia between the circular and longitudinal muscle layers that controls motility.
Failure of the lower esophageal sphincter to relax with swallowing, together with loss of peristalsis in the esophageal body.
Failure of propulsion through the intestine without any physical blockage of the lumen.
A physical block inside, within the wall of, or outside the bowel that prevents passage of contents.
The site on imaging where dilated bowel above a mechanical obstruction changes to collapsed bowel below it.
A hernia whose contents are trapped and cannot be returned to the abdomen.
An incarcerated or twisted segment whose blood supply is compromised, leading to ischemia and infarction.
A segment blocked at both ends, as in volvulus, so pressure rises quickly and threatens its blood supply.
Telescoping of a proximal segment of bowel (the intussusceptum) into the adjacent distal segment (the intussuscipiens).
Twisting of a loop of bowel around the axis of its mesentery, obstructing both the lumen and the vessels.
An outpouching made of mucosa and submucosa only, without the muscularis propria.
A lowered threshold for perceiving gut distension or contraction as painful, central to irritable bowel syndrome.

sections.title: Achalasia: loss of inhibitory neurons in the esophagus

blocks.text: The lower esophageal sphincter (LES) is a zone of tonically contracted smooth muscle at the gastroesophageal (GE) junction. Its resting tone comes from the muscle itself and from excitatory cholinergic neurons. When a person swallows, vagal fibers activate inhibitory neurons of the myenteric plexus, which release nitric oxide (NO) and vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP). These relax the LES within seconds and also produce the timed wave of inhibition that lets peristalsis travel down the smooth muscle esophagus in order.

Achalasia is the selective loss of these inhibitory neurons. In primary (idiopathic) achalasia the myenteric ganglia show inflammation, mainly T lymphocytes, and fibrosis; an autoimmune response, possibly triggered by a viral infection in a genetically susceptible person, is the leading hypothesis. Excitatory cholinergic input is relatively spared, so it is left unopposed. The LES has normal or raised resting pressure and relaxes incompletely or not at all, and the distal esophagus loses peristalsis because the inhibitory wave that sequences contraction is gone.

blocks.title: From neuron loss to the bird-beak esophagus
steps: Inflammation destroys NO and VIP neurons of the myenteric plexus
Excitatory cholinergic tone is left unopposed
LES fails to relax on swallowing
Esophageal body loses ordered peristalsis
Food and fluid pool above a closed LES
Esophagus dilates and tapers to a narrow beak
blocks.caption: The obstruction is functional: the lumen at the LES is anatomically normal but does not open.

blocks.text: Because the problem is a sphincter that will not open rather than a narrowed lumen, solids and liquids are both held up from the start. Patients also describe regurgitation of undigested food, chest discomfort, nocturnal cough or aspiration, and gradual weight loss. A barium swallow shows a dilated esophagus, often with an air-fluid level, tapering smoothly to a bird beak at the GE junction; a chest film may show a widened mediastinum and a small or absent gastric air bubble. Esophageal manometry is the defining test, showing incomplete LES relaxation with absent peristalsis. Long-standing stasis and chronic mucosal irritation raise the risk of squamous cell carcinoma.

Secondary achalasia has the same physiology from a known cause. In Chagas disease, Trypanosoma cruzi, transmitted by triatomine bugs in Latin America, destroys enteric ganglia over years and can produce megaesophagus, megacolon, and cardiomyopathy in the same patient. A tumor at the GE junction can infiltrate the plexus and mimic the picture (pseudoachalasia), which is suspected in an older patient with rapid weight loss and a short history.

blocks.title: Achalasia compared with other causes of esophageal dysphagia
blocks.caption: Motility disorders affect solids and liquids together; a fixed narrowing blocks solids first.

blocks.predict: Manometry shows absent distal peristalsis in two patients. One has an LES that will not relax; the other has a very weak LES and severe heartburn. Which has lost neurons and which has lost muscle?
blocks.explain: The first has achalasia: muscle is present but its inhibitory innervation is gone, so tone persists and relaxation fails. The second has systemic sclerosis: fibrosis replaces the smooth muscle itself, so the LES cannot generate tone and acid refluxes freely.

sections.title: Adynamic ileus compared with mechanical obstruction

blocks.text: Moving contents along the intestine needs three things: intact enteric neurons, excitable smooth muscle, and a balance of autonomic input in which parasympathetic activity promotes and sympathetic activity inhibits motility. Obstruction results either when propulsion fails with an open lumen (adynamic, or paralytic, ileus) or when the lumen is physically blocked (mechanical obstruction).

Adynamic ileus is a global failure of motility. After abdominal surgery, spinal and prevertebral sympathetic reflexes inhibit the enteric plexus, and handling of the bowel activates macrophages in the muscularis that release inflammatory mediators, including NO and prostaglandins, which suppress contraction. Peritonitis acts through the same inflammatory route. Hypokalemia hyperpolarizes smooth muscle cells, moving the membrane away from threshold so slow waves fail to trigger spikes. Opioids bind mu receptors on enteric neurons and reduce acetylcholine release, so propulsion stops while nonpropulsive segmental tone may increase. Because no segment is blocked, gas spreads through small and large bowel, the abdomen is distended but pain is mild, and bowel sounds are reduced or absent.

In mechanical obstruction the bowel above the block is still innervated and contracts harder against it, producing cramping (colicky) pain and high-pitched, tinkling sounds as fluid and gas are forced through a narrowed segment. Below the block the bowel empties and collapses, which creates the transition point on imaging. In adults, adhesions from previous surgery are the most common cause of small bowel obstruction, followed by hernias; colorectal cancer is the most common cause of large bowel obstruction. Fecal impaction blocks the lumen from within, and a gallstone lodged at the ileocecal valve (gallstone ileus) is mechanical despite its name.

rows: Gas in small and large bowel, no transition point

blocks.caption: A late mechanical obstruction can fall silent as the bowel fatigues, so the transition point is the more reliable distinction.

blocks.title: Why prolonged mechanical obstruction becomes dangerous
steps: Gas and secretions accumulate above the block
Distension raises wall tension
Mucosal perfusion falls; secretion exceeds absorption
Vomiting and fluid sequestration cause hypovolemia
Stasis allows bacterial overgrowth and translocation

blocks.caption: By the law of Laplace, wall tension rises with radius, so the most dilated segment is most at risk.

blocks.title: Worked example: electrolytes after repeated vomiting
blocks.text: A patient with a high small bowel obstruction vomits for two days. Gastric HCl is lost, so bicarbonate generated by parietal cells stays in the blood: metabolic alkalosis with low chloride. Volume loss activates the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system. Aldosterone drives Na+ reabsorption in the collecting duct in exchange for K+ and H+, so urinary K+ loss causes hypokalemia, and the urine can be acidic despite systemic alkalosis (paradoxical aciduria). The hypokalemia then hyperpolarizes intestinal smooth muscle and adds an adynamic component to the mechanical block.

sections.title: Hiatal hernias and strangulation of abdominal wall hernias

blocks.text: Sliding and paraesophageal hiatal hernias

The esophagus passes through the esophageal hiatus, a sling formed by the right crus of the diaphragm, and is held in place by the phrenoesophageal ligament. Normally a short segment of the LES sits below the diaphragm, where intra-abdominal pressure and the crural sling both add to its barrier against reflux. A hiatal hernia forms when the hiatus widens and the ligament stretches, which becomes more likely with age, obesity, and anything that raises intra-abdominal pressure.

In a sliding hernia, by far the most common type, the GE junction and cardia move up into the thorax. The LES is separated from the crural sling and loses its intra-abdominal segment, so the antireflux barrier weakens and gastroesophageal reflux follows. In a paraesophageal hernia the GE junction stays anchored below the diaphragm, so reflux is less prominent, but the fundus rolls up through the hiatus beside the esophagus. That herniated stomach can twist (gastric volvulus), become trapped, bleed, or strangulate.

blocks.title: Sliding and paraesophageal hiatal hernias
blocks.caption: Mixed hernias combine an elevated GE junction with herniated fundus.

blocks.text: From incarceration to strangulation

An abdominal wall hernia is reducible when its contents can be returned, incarcerated when they are trapped, and strangulated when trapped contents lose their blood supply. The order of events follows vessel pressures. Mesenteric veins have thin walls and low pressure, so the tight hernia neck compresses them first while arterial blood still flows in. Blood is trapped, capillary hydrostatic pressure rises, and fluid leaks into the wall and lumen. The segment swells, which tightens the neck further, until tissue pressure exceeds arterial pressure and inflow stops.

blocks.title: Strangulation of an incarcerated hernia
steps: Bowel trapped in a narrow hernia neck
Thin-walled veins compressed; arterial inflow continues
Venous congestion and edema swell the segment
Swelling tightens the neck; arterial inflow stops
Hemorrhagic infarction of the trapped bowel
Perforation, peritonitis, and sepsis
blocks.caption: Venous obstruction comes before arterial obstruction, so strangulated bowel is dark, swollen, and hemorrhagic.

blocks.text: Strangulation changes the picture from intermittent colic to constant, severe pain with a tense, tender, often discolored hernia that cannot be reduced, followed by fever, tachycardia, leukocytosis, and lactic acidosis as the bowel dies and bacteria cross the damaged wall. Femoral hernias carry the highest risk among groin hernias because the femoral ring is narrow and bounded by unyielding structures: the inguinal ligament in front, the lacunar ligament medially, and the pectineal ligament behind.

blocks.predict: Why does strangulated bowel look dark red and swollen rather than pale?
blocks.explain: The veins close first while arteries still pump blood in, so the segment fills with blood and edema before inflow finally stops. The result is a hemorrhagic (red) infarct, not a pale one.
blocks.check: The strangulation flow and the paragraph before it.

blocks.text: Both cause mechanical obstruction and threaten the blood supply, because the mesentery and its vessels are dragged into or twisted with the bowel.
Intussusception

Peristalsis grips a mass in the bowel wall, the lead point, and pulls it with its segment and mesentery into the bowel just ahead. The usual site is ileocolic, with terminal ileum entering the cecum. It is the most common cause of intestinal obstruction in children about 6 months to 3 years old. In most children the lead point is lymphoid hyperplasia of Peyer patches after a viral infection, especially adenovirus; a Meckel diverticulum, polyp, lymphoma, or the bowel wall hemorrhage of IgA vasculitis can also serve. In adults a definable lead point, usually a tumor, is present in most cases.

The trapped mesentery is compressed, so venous and lymphatic outflow fail first, the wall becomes edematous, and congested mucosa sheds blood mixed with mucus, the currant jelly stool. This is a sign of mucosal ischemia and tends to appear late. Typical findings are bouts of severe colicky pain with the legs drawn up and calm periods between, a sausage-shaped mass, often in the right upper quadrant, and a target sign on ultrasound from concentric rings of bowel wall.
Volvulus

In volvulus a loop rotates around its mesenteric axis. This creates a closed-loop obstruction and kinks the mesenteric vessels at the same time, so ischemia develops early. A twist needs a mobile loop on a narrow mesenteric base. In older adults that is a long, redundant sigmoid colon, favored by chronic constipation; imaging shows a hugely dilated loop shaped like a coffee bean. In infants it is malrotation: the midgut fails to complete its 270 degree counterclockwise rotation around the superior mesenteric artery, leaving the small bowel on a narrow pedicle and often with peritoneal (Ladd) bands crossing the duodenum. Midgut volvulus can infarct the whole territory of the superior mesenteric artery.

sections.title: Causes of megacolon: Hirschsprung disease, Chagas disease, and toxic megacolon

blocks.text: Megacolon means marked dilation of the colon. The three classic causes reach it by different routes: absence of neurons from birth, destruction of neurons later in life, or acute paralysis of inflamed muscle.
Hirschsprung disease

Enteric neurons come from vagal neural crest cells that migrate down the gut from cranial to caudal between about weeks 5 and 12 of development. If migration stops early, the distal bowel has no ganglion cells in either the myenteric or the submucosal plexus. Because migration proceeds in one direction, the aganglionic segment always includes the rectum and extends upward as one continuous segment, most often confined to the rectosigmoid. Loss-of-function mutations in RET, the tyrosine kinase receptor in the glial cell line derived neurotrophic factor pathway, are the main genetic cause, and the disease is more common in boys and in Down syndrome.

blocks.title: Hirschsprung disease from embryology to presentation
steps: Neural crest cells fail to reach the distal bowel
Rectum and adjoining segment lack ganglion cells
No NO and VIP release; segment cannot relax
Aganglionic segment acts as a functional obstruction
Normal colon above it dilates
Delayed meconium, distension, empty rectal vault
blocks.caption: The narrow segment is the diseased part; the dilated colon above it is normally innervated.

blocks.text: A newborn fails to pass meconium within 48 hours and develops abdominal distension and bilious vomiting. On rectal examination the vault is empty and tight, and withdrawing the finger often releases explosive gas and stool. Anorectal manometry shows loss of the rectoanal inhibitory reflex, the internal sphincter relaxation that normally follows rectal distension. Rectal suction biopsy confirms the diagnosis by showing no ganglion cells, with hypertrophied nerve trunks and increased acetylcholinesterase staining. Stasis predisposes to enterocolitis.
Chagas disease and toxic megacolon

In chronic Chagas disease, Trypanosoma cruzi infection destroys enteric ganglia, so the colon and esophagus lose inhibitory control in adult life; a patient from Latin America with megacolon, megaesophagus, and dilated cardiomyopathy fits this pattern. Toxic megacolon is different: severe colitis, classically ulcerative colitis or Clostridioides difficile colitis, extends transmurally into the muscularis propria. Inflammatory NO and neuronal injury paralyze the muscle, the colon dilates (commonly defined as more than about 6 cm), and systemic toxicity follows with fever, tachycardia, and leukocytosis. The thinned wall can perforate. Hypokalemia and opioid or anticholinergic drugs that reduce motility can precipitate it.

blocks.title: Causes of megacolon
rows: Congenital absence of ganglion cells, rectum upward
Newborn, delayed meconium, empty rectal vault

blocks.caption: Two are neural (absent or destroyed ganglia); one is inflammatory paralysis of muscle.

blocks.predict: A contrast enema in a newborn shows a narrow rectum and a widely dilated sigmoid. Which segment would a biopsy show to be abnormal?
blocks.explain: The narrow rectum. It lacks ganglion cells and cannot relax, so it obstructs; the dilated colon above has normal ganglia and is distended only because contents cannot pass.

blocks.text: A true diverticulum contains all layers of the wall, including the muscularis propria, as a Meckel diverticulum does. A false diverticulum is mucosa and submucosa pushed out through a gap in the muscle. Pulsion diverticula are false and form where pressure inside the lumen is high and the muscle wall has a weak spot; traction diverticula are true and form where scarring outside the wall pulls it outward.

The inferior pharyngeal constrictor has two parts: the oblique thyropharyngeus above and the horizontal cricopharyngeus below, which forms most of the upper esophageal sphincter. Between them on the posterior wall lies a triangle of thin muscle (Killian triangle). Zenker diverticulum is a pulsion, false diverticulum that herniates through this weak area, just above the cricopharyngeus.

The driving problem is cricopharyngeal dysfunction. With age the cricopharyngeus becomes fibrotic and less compliant, so it does not open fully when the pharynx contracts. Pressure in the hypopharynx rises with every swallow, and over years mucosa and submucosa bulge backward through the weak triangle, usually in adults over about 60.

blocks.title: Formation of a Zenker diverticulum
steps: Cricopharyngeus becomes fibrotic and opens incompletely
Hypopharyngeal pressure rises with each swallow
Mucosa and submucosa bulge through Killian triangle
Pouch enlarges and retains food
Pouch contents regurgitate, decay, or are aspirated
blocks.caption: The pouch lies posteriorly above the upper esophageal sphincter, so it fills before the bolus can enter the esophagus.

blocks.text: The symptoms follow from a pouch that fills during swallowing and empties later. Dysphagia is oropharyngeal, felt high in the neck. Food that sat in the pouch returns undigested, sometimes hours after a meal, and bacterial breakdown of retained food causes halitosis. Patients may notice gurgling in the neck or a soft neck mass, and spillover into the larynx, especially when lying down, causes cough and aspiration pneumonia. A barium swallow shows the posterior pouch. Endoscopy carries a risk of perforation because the scope can enter the pouch rather than the esophagus.

blocks.title: Esophageal diverticula by location
rows: Pulled out by fibrosis of nearby lymph nodes, as after tuberculosis or histoplasmosis
Pulsion from distal motility disorders such as achalasia
blocks.caption: Pulsion diverticula are false; traction diverticula are true.

blocks.text: Both are motility disorders without a physical block. Irritable bowel syndrome (IBS), unlike gastroparesis, has no structural or biochemical marker and is defined by symptoms.
Gastroparesis

Normal gastric emptying depends on vagally mediated relaxation of the fundus to accept a meal, rhythmic antral contractions paced by slow waves from the interstitial cells of Cajal (ICC) that grind solids, and coordinated opening of the pylorus. Gastroparesis is delayed emptying of solids without mechanical obstruction. Diabetes mellitus is a leading cause, most often type 1 of long duration. Autonomic neuropathy damages vagal fibers, the stomach loses ICC and myenteric neurons that make neuronal NO synthase, and antral contractions weaken while the pylorus fails to relax. Acute hyperglycemia itself also slows emptying. Other causes include vagotomy, systemic sclerosis, and drugs that slow motility such as opioids, and many cases are idiopathic.

Food stays in the stomach, so patients have early satiety, postprandial fullness, bloating, nausea, and vomiting of food eaten hours earlier; retained material can form a bezoar. In a person with diabetes, absorption of a meal no longer matches the timing of insulin, producing erratic glucose levels with unexpected hypoglycemia. Diagnosis requires excluding obstruction by endoscopy and then demonstrating delayed emptying of a solid meal, usually by scintigraphy.
Irritable bowel syndrome

IBS is a disorder of gut-brain interaction. Its core is visceral hypersensitivity, in which normal distension and contraction are felt as pain, together with altered motility and abnormal central processing of visceral signals. Contributors include changes in the gut microbiota, low-grade mucosal immune activation with mast cells near nerve endings, altered serotonin signaling from enterochromaffin cells, and psychological stress. A subset begins after acute infectious gastroenteritis (post-infectious IBS). It is more common in women.

The Rome IV definition is recurrent abdominal pain, on average at least one day a week for three months, with at least two of: relation to defecation, a change in stool frequency, or a change in stool form, and onset at least six months before diagnosis. Subtypes (constipation, diarrhea, mixed, or unclassified) follow the dominant stool form. Because IBS leaves the bowel structurally normal, weight loss, bleeding, or anemia indicates another disease.

integration.text: Most conditions in this chapter come down to one question: is the enteric nervous system missing, damaged, or overridden, or is the lumen physically closed? Embryology explains the congenital forms, with failed neural crest migration in Hirschsprung disease and incomplete midgut rotation in malrotation. Microbiology adds Trypanosoma cruzi, which removes ganglia in the esophagus and colon, and Clostridioides difficile, which can paralyze an inflamed colon. Immunology underlies the ganglionitis of primary achalasia and the colitis behind toxic megacolon. Physiology explains why the same loss of NO and VIP neurons produces a sphincter that will not open in the esophagus and a segment that will not relax in the rectum.

Pathology ties the mechanical disorders to ischemia. Hernias, intussusception, and volvulus all compress or twist the mesentery, and because veins close before arteries, the result is a swollen, hemorrhagic infarct that can perforate. Systemic consequences link to renal and acid-base physiology: vomiting, sequestration, and aldosterone produce hypovolemia, hypokalemia, and alkalosis, and the hypokalemia feeds back to slow the bowel further. The limits of the pattern matter too: a late mechanical obstruction can be silent like an ileus, and IBS is a diagnosis made only after structural disease has been excluded.

summary: Achalasia is loss of inhibitory NO and VIP myenteric neurons, so the LES fails to relax and peristalsis is lost; dysphagia to solids and liquids, bird-beak swallow, Chagas disease as a secondary cause.
Systemic sclerosis also abolishes distal peristalsis but leaves a weak LES with reflux, because muscle, not nerve, is lost.

Adynamic ileus is global loss of propulsion (surgery, peritonitis, hypokalemia, opioids) with absent sounds and diffuse gas; mechanical obstruction has colicky pain, high-pitched sounds, and a transition point.
Sliding hiatal hernias lift the GE junction and cause reflux; paraesophageal hernias leave it in place and risk volvulus and strangulation.
Strangulation follows venous compression, edema, then arterial occlusion, producing a hemorrhagic infarct; femoral hernias carry the highest risk.
Intussusception is usually ileocolic in children about 6 months to 3 years with a lead point, colicky pain, a sausage mass, and currant jelly stool.
Volvulus is twisting on the mesentery: sigmoid in older constipated adults (coffee bean sign), midgut with malrotation in infants (bilious vomiting).
Hirschsprung disease is congenital absence of ganglion cells beginning at the rectum; the narrow segment is diseased and the dilated colon above is normal.
Zenker diverticulum is a false pulsion diverticulum through Killian triangle above a poorly opening cricopharyngeus, causing regurgitation of undigested food and halitosis.
Diabetic gastroparesis delays gastric emptying through vagal neuropathy and ICC loss; IBS is pain linked to defecation with altered stool form and no structural disease.
